title: Confidence and Longing in Danger
overview: A person surrounded by enemies declares trust in the LORD, longs to stay near God, and then pleads not to be abandoned.

parts.label: Nothing to fear (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The poet, traditionally linked to King David, calls the LORD his light, his rescue and his fortress, so even an army camped against him cannot shake his confidence. The enemies who come to 'devour' him like wild animals are the ones who stumble and fall.

parts.label: The one thing he wants (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: His single request is to live close to God in God's house, called here both a temple and a sacred tent, to gaze on the LORD's beauty and to seek him there. He pictures that place as a hiding spot and a high rock, and promises joyful offerings and songs once he is lifted above his enemies.

parts.label: A sudden turn to pleading (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: The calm confidence gives way to urgent prayer, and some scholars think two poems were joined here, while others read it as one person's shifting moods. To 'seek God's face' means to seek God's favor and attention, and he trusts that even if his own parents abandoned him, the LORD would take him in.

parts.label: Lied about and hunted (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: He asks to be led on a straight, level path because his enemies are watching for him to fall. They use false testimony against him, which in that world could cost a person their reputation or even their life.

parts.label: Waiting with courage (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: In the original language verse 13 reads like an unfinished sentence, which may show how strongly he feels as he trusts he will see the LORD's goodness in this life, 'the land of the living.' The closing lines urge waiting for the LORD with strength and courage, said twice for emphasis.

think: If you could ask for only one thing to hold onto when life feels threatening, what would it be, and why that?
